claims.text: Sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles initially form a metastable single-phase solid solution or chemically disordered state.
Above 600 K, surface-mediated kinetics overwhelm the hypothesized high-entropy sluggish-diffusion effect in these nanoparticles.
Surface-energy-driven segregation drives the structural evolution during heating.
Ostwald ripening drives the loss of the smallest particles.
Surface-energy minimization produces particle shape anisotropy.
The high surface-to-volume ratio creates a large surface-energy gradient in sub-10 nm particles.
The surface-energy gradient lowers the activation barrier for surface diffusion relative to bulk diffusion.
High curvature gives smaller particles a higher chemical potential through the Gibbs-Thomson effect.
The curvature-induced chemical-potential difference transports mass from smaller particles to larger particles.
Surface-mediated mass transport is faster than the bulk diffusion needed to preserve a single-phase alloy.
The heated nanoparticles undergo rapid phase separation.
Low-surface-energy Au or Pt segregates to nanoparticle surfaces.
Au or Pt may instead form larger stable cores.
The smallest particles dissolve completely during heating.
The number density of particles smaller than 5 nm falls to near zero by 800 K.
Larger particles grow and become faceted during heating.
The remaining particles deviate from equiatomic bulk composition.
The remaining particles become enriched in the element having the lowest surface energy.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion would otherwise preserve a single-phase equiatomic structure up to 1000 K.
For particles larger than 50 nm, surface driving forces are insufficient for rapid segregation and sluggish diffusion may preserve the single-phase structure.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes segregation to minimization of surface free energy and predicts that low-surface-energy Au or Pt will occupy the surface, but also proposes that the same components may form stable cores without identifying an additional driving force that would favor core placement.
